# How Studies Go Wrong

::: {.callout-note}

-   Recognize the recurring measurement traps in AI-productivity studies.
-   Match a vendor claim to the specific trap it's falling into.
-   Diagnose why self-report, selection bias, and weak baselines mislead.

:::

Meridian's team spends an afternoon reading the vendor's evidence pack. Priya
walks them through a dozen charts, each one showing the tool in a flattering
light. Maya, Dev, and Jonas each find themselves nodding at a different chart —
for a different bad reason.

The traps below are the most common ways AI-productivity studies go wrong. At
least one of them is almost certainly operating in *your* organization right
now. Each has a one-line **tell** — a phrase or number that should make you
reach for this chapter.

## Timing Artificial Tasks

The famous "55% faster" result came from a single greenfield task: implement an
HTTP server in JavaScript, from scratch, in ninety minutes [@Peng2023]. Real
software development is navigating a codebase someone else wrote, interpreting
an ambiguous ticket, coordinating with three colleagues, and sitting in four
meetings. Speed on a toy task doesn't predict speed on any of that.

**Tell:** the task is greenfield, time-boxed to under a day, and done by
developers with no other obligations. Jonas is the character most likely to fall
for this — toy tasks are exactly where the tool makes him *feel* fast.

## Measuring Only the Easy Half

Code generation gets faster, and that half is easy to measure. The other half is
harder: time spent reviewing AI output for correctness, time lost debugging
confident-but-wrong suggestions, security holes in plausible-looking code, and
technical debt from suggestions that solved the immediate problem while ignoring
the design around it [@Pearce2022]. A 2025 evaluation of five major LLMs found
that *none* produced web-application code meeting industry security standards
[@Dora2025]. If AI raises code volume without raising review capacity, cycle time
can *worsen*.

**Tell:** the study measures time-to-first-code, not time-to-merged, and never
mentions review, defects, or rework. Dev's dashboard — PRs merged — is this trap
in spreadsheet form.

## Before/After With No Control Group

You roll out the tool in January; by June, PRs ship faster. Also between January
and June: you hired three developers, rewrote the CI pipeline, and switched
cloud providers. Without a group that *didn't* get the tool, you can't separate
the AI effect from everything else that changed.

**Tell:** there is no comparison team, or the "control" is the same team in the
past. Dev's "PRs up 18%" is a before/after with no counterfactual.

## Asking Developers If They Feel More Productive

"87% of developers report feeling more productive with AI" gets cited as proof
that the tool works [@Liang2024]. Three things make self-report systematically
misleading: the {{<g novelty_effect "novelty effect" >}} (new tools feel fast
until the shine wears off), the {{<g hawthorne_effect "Hawthorne effect" >}}
(people perform differently when observed), and {{<g social_desirability_bias
"social desirability bias" >}} (people tell the survey what it wants to hear,
especially when management picked the tool). Feeling faster isn't being faster.

**Tell:** the headline number is "X% *report* feeling more productive," not a
measured outcome. Jonas is the poster child for this one.

## Treating Adoption Rate as a Success Metric

"We've hit 90% adoption across engineering" is a procurement outcome, not a
productivity outcome. Adoption measures whether the tool is installed and
opened — not whether suggestions are useful, whether they're accepted
thoughtlessly, or whether the accepted ones are correct. Adoption is easier to
measure than benefit, which is exactly why it gets reported instead.

**Tell:** the number is "adoption," "seats," or "activation," not any outcome.
Priya leads with this chart.

## Comparing Volunteers to Non-Volunteers

A study that compares developers who *chose* to use AI against those who didn't
is comparing two different populations, not two conditions. Early adopters are
more motivated to experiment, more comfortable with new tools, and more likely
to already be high performers. {{<g selection_bias "Selection bias" >}} means
any difference may be a property of the person, not the tool. This is the single
most common flaw in industry AI-productivity reports — a two-year longitudinal
study found Copilot users were already more active than non-users *before* the
tool was introduced [@Stray2026].

**Tell:** the groups self-selected; nobody was randomly assigned. If Dev had let
developers "opt in" to the rollout, his numbers would carry this flaw.

## Treating Suggestion Acceptance Rate as a Quality Signal

Assistants report what fraction of their suggestions developers accept, and
vendors present a rising acceptance rate as a quality improvement. Acceptance
measures whether the code looked plausible enough to press Tab — not whether it
was correct, secure, or maintainable. Field reports from companies like ZoomInfo
lean on acceptance-rate figures for exactly this reason [@Bakal2025]. Under time
pressure, developers accept *more* suggestions, including insecure ones
[@Pearce2022].

**Tell:** the metric is "acceptance rate" or "suggestions shown." A rising
acceptance rate is often a signal that people stopped reading.

## Comparing AI to Nothing

A study that compares AI-assisted developers to a control group using *nothing*
has chosen a baseline that doesn't exist in practice. Developers without an AI
assistant still use Stack Overflow, docs, and their teammates. The relevant
question is whether the AI tool beats those alternatives, not whether it beats
sitting in silence.

**Tell:** the control group "used no assistance" rather than "used the tools
developers already have." Any tool looks good against nothing.

## The Tells at a Glance

Paste this on the wall next to your dashboard:

-   Greenfield task under a day → **artificial task**
-   Time-to-first-code, no review/rework → **easy half**
-   No comparison team → **no control group**
-   "% report feeling faster" → **self-report**
-   "adoption / seats / activation" → **procurement, not productivity**
-   Groups self-selected → **selection bias**
-   "acceptance rate" → **plausibility, not quality**
-   Control used nothing → **weak baseline**

## Check Understanding

<details markdown="1">
<summary markdown="1">Your company surveys developers three weeks after rolling out an AI assistant; 78% report feeling more productive. Dev says this proves it works. Name two specific flaws.</summary>

First, three weeks falls inside the novelty period, when enthusiasm inflates
self-report regardless of real performance. Second, feeling productive is not
being productive — self-report is distorted by the Hawthorne effect and social
desirability bias, especially when management chose the tool.

</details>

<details markdown="1">
<summary markdown="1">A study compares fifty developers who volunteered to use an AI assistant against fifty who didn't. The AI group closes 25% more tickets. What's the likely alternative explanation, and what design change fixes it?</summary>

Selection bias: volunteers differ from non-volunteers in ways that predict
productivity independent of the tool. Random assignment — giving the tool to a
random half of developers — makes the groups comparable on average.

</details>

<details markdown="1">
<summary markdown="1">A vendor's acceptance rate rose from 25% to 40% last quarter, which they call a "quality improvement." What's wrong with that reading?</summary>

Acceptance measures whether a suggestion looked plausible, not whether it was
correct, secure, or maintainable. A rise can reflect better suggestions — or
more time pressure, simpler tasks, or habituation. Without a separate quality
measure, acceptance rate says nothing about whether the code got better.

</details>

<details markdown="1">
<summary markdown="1">"We'll measure lines of code per developer per week, two weeks before and after adoption." Identify at least two flaws.</summary>

Lines of code has low construct validity as a productivity measure, and a
two-week window sits entirely inside the novelty period. A better design uses an
outcome-linked metric (deployment frequency plus change failure rate, or cycle
time) over at least three to six months, with a team that didn't adopt the tool
as a control.

</details>

## Exercises

### Spot the Trap (20 minutes, pairs)

For each vendor claim below, name the trap from this chapter it's falling into,
and write one sentence on what you'd need to see to actually evaluate it:

1.  "Teams using our assistant merged 23% more pull requests last quarter."
2.  "92% of developers say they feel more productive with our tool."
3.  "Our acceptance rate hit 41%, up from 27% a year ago."
4.  "Adoption across your engineering org is now 88%."
5.  "In our study, developers with the tool finished a coding task 30% faster
    than those without it."

### Audit Your Own Dashboard (15 minutes, solo)

List three metrics your organization currently uses (or has recently used) to
judge a tool or process change. For each, name the trap from this chapter it
falls into — or, if it avoids them all, say in one sentence why.

### Redesign One Flawed Study (15 minutes, pairs)

A company plans to "survey developers about perceived productivity after two
weeks, compare to a pre-adoption survey, and report the percentage who feel more
productive." Identify three problems, then in a few sentences describe a better
design: what to measure, over what period, and how to build a comparison group.
